proposals.approach: The date is the sheet's own due date. The default calendar of pages per year and half term already fixes which sheets a Year 8, 9 or 10 fills in each half term. The app gives each of those sheets a date by which it is to be scríofa, rewritten from memory and sent to the teacher (Seol chuig an mhúinteoir), and prints that date in the candidate box as the third cell: Bileog 2a / faoi 23 Deireadh Fómhair. The pupil prepares for sending the sheet, not for a meeting. Nothing is staged on a day: the school's half-term dates are the only calendar input, the teacher receives the sent card at the address on the cover and corrects it in their own time, and the pupil enters the correction (Ceart mar atá, or the teacher's line) when it comes back. Sending is the pupil's act that moves a line to box 4; the teacher's reading, once entered, is what moves it to box 5. The partner, the card tick and An comhrá go; Years 11 and 12 keep Scrúdú and the exam month, with the same due dates shown on their sheets in An scríbhinn only. The rule for a due date: the half term's last school night is the due date of its last sheet; where a half term holds more than one sheet, the earlier sheets fall due on the Friday that divides the half term's school nights in proportion to their line counts; a sheet of fewer than four lines shares the next sheet's date; a date typed from the board on the cover replaces the default for that sheet; at first open, any default already past is moved to the Friday a fortnight on. The same six dates per school year that the brief's conversation defaults already used (the last school night of each half term) are the whole data need, so departmentPages.json changes shape, not size.
proposals.dateCell:
Cell shape unchanged: a label and a value. Label is Bileog and the sheet reference, value is faoi and the date, Ulster month names, no year (the year is on the stamp). The sheet shown is the earliest unsent sheet on the year's calendar; the cell stays on it, date past or not, until Seol chuig an mhúinteoir completes, then moves to the next. Worked from the usual NI autumn half term 2026 (school nights Tuesday 1 September to Friday 23 October, 39 nights):

Year 8, 8B, first half term, sheets 1a (8 lines) and 2a (12 lines): before 1a is sent the cell reads Bileog 1a / faoi 25 Meán Fómhair (8/20 of 39 nights ends Tuesday 22 September; the Friday on or after is 25 September); once 1a is sent it reads Bileog 2a / faoi 23 Deireadh Fómhair (the last school night). English gloss beneath in grey for Years 8 and 9: Sheet 1a, by 25 September.

Year 9, 9B, first half term, sheets 1b (12 lines, Mé féin tier 2) and 2b (School tier 2, count to be fixed by the tier sign-off, about 12): Bileog 1b / faoi 2 Deireadh Fómhair (half the nights ends Monday 28 September, Friday 2 October follows), then Bileog 2b / faoi 23 Deireadh Fómhair.

Year 10, 10B, first half term, sheets 1c (1 line, Q021) and the School tier-3 sheet: 1c has fewer than four lines so it shares the next sheet's date; the cell reads Bileog 1c / faoi 23 Deireadh Fómhair and then Bileog 2d / faoi 23 Deireadh Fómhair (2d being whatever letter the School tier-3 cut takes).

Years 11 and 12 unchanged: Scrúdú / Bealtaine 2028 and Scrúdú / Bealtaine 2027.

Where the date comes from: departmentPages.json carries, per school year, the six last school nights of the half terms (the school's published calendar, which exists whether or not the app does) and the pages per half term already accepted; the app derives each sheet's due date by the rule in the approach, no server; a date typed on the cover from the board overrides one sheet's default. The word faoi (by) is used as the approach gives it; Dáithí to rule whether Ulster fá or roimh is wanted instead, since he signs every string.
proposals.whatIsPreparedFor: The Year 8 is working towards sending sheet 1a, then 2a, to their own teacher by a printed date: eight lines about themselves in biro, each one rewritten from memory at least once, sent as a card with Mo cheist at the foot, and their teacher's red pen coming back on it. That is real because the teacher, the address and the date all exist outside the app (the date is the school's own half-term calendar), and it is dated without the school staging anything, because the department promised only what it can keep, that a teacher who receives a sent sheet will correct it in their own time. A 12-year-old opens the app tomorrow because the sheet is an object that fills one line a night and the date it must be full by is printed on every screen and is close; because last night's fada! is retested tonight, not next week; because the stamp says maith thú, Sin é anocht, and nothing else is asked; and because when the card comes back with the teacher's handwriting on it, the app is where that correction goes, and the corrected line comes round the next night to be written right, which is the one moment a Year 8 sees the teacher's mark and their own line meet. The conversation is still what every line is for, and the cover still says so; it is only no longer the thing with the date.
proposals.boxGate:
Boxes 0 to 3 as the brief has them: a right Athscríobh from memory advances the box up to 3. Box 3 to box 4: the line's sheet has been sent (Seol chuig an mhúinteoir completed, flag tugtha isteach) and one further right rewrite from memory is written after the sending; the line is stamped seolta. Box 4 to box 5: the teacher's reading of that line has been entered from the returned card, either Ceart mar atá (the teacher ticked the box or left the rule blank) or Ceartú an mhúinteora typed in as a draft of kind teacher, and a right rewrite from memory follows; if a correction was typed, the line first drops to box 0 with the teacher's line as the key, so box 5 is reached only after the corrected form has been written right twice more. Missed rewrite, arís, or Athscríobh le cuidiú set box 0 as before. No recording is involved anywhere in the gate; Abair é stays unmarked and moves no box until Abair.

Why it is honest: the pen can check fadas, mutations and listed words, and it never claims more; box 3 is where the pen's own judgement runs out. What moves a line past it is not a machine judgement of speech. Box 4 rests on the pupil's own act: sending the sheet is standing over the line as their best, in front of a reader who exists, and the app records the act, not a verdict. Box 5 rests on the only human reading in the loop, the teacher's, which is a stronger judgement than the partner's tick was (right as written, not merely understood when said), and it is entered by the pupil from a real card, never inferred. What the app therefore never claims for a Year 8 to 10 line is that it has been said to anyone; it claims written right, sent, read. If the teacher never replies, the line's ceiling is box 4 and the app leaves it there rather than pretend; that ceiling is the pupil's own to reach.
proposals.teacherLeg:
Sending: on the sheet in An scríbhinn, once it is scríofa and ó chuimhne (every line written and rewritten from memory), the foot action Seol chuig an mhúinteoir renders the card (candidate box with the Bileog and faoi date, hand line, each question in print, the pupil's line beneath, a tick box for the teacher labelled Ceart mar atá, a blank rule for the teacher's correction, Mo cheist at the foot) as an A4 PDF into the share sheet with the teacher's address from the cover prefilled (email or Teams drop, one string per class); Priontáil is the second choice for a pupil who hands the paper in. The flag tugtha isteach is set and the sheet stamped seolta on completion; the cover cell moves to the next sheet. The app offers it when the sheet is ready and the due date is within a week, and again if the date passes unsent; it never withholds sending, and a sheet sent late is simply sent.

Correcting: the teacher opens the PDF or the printed card whenever they like, ticks Ceart mar atá or writes a correction on the rule for each line, answers Mo cheist if they wish, and returns it by the same channel or hands it back in class. Nothing is collected on a day and no date is promised.

Entering: the pupil, with the returned card, opens the sheet and its foot action is now Ceartú ar ais; each line offers Ceart mar atá (one tap: teacherRead recorded as ceart) or Scríobh ceartú an mhúinteora (the teacher's line typed on the rule, with strict fadas and the FadaToolbar, saved as a draft of kind teacher that becomes the line's key, one tap choosing fada, séimhiú, urú, ainm briathartha or focal for Le ceartú; the line goes to box 0 and comes up as item 1 the next night). A line with no mark from the teacher is left untouched, not guessed. When every line has a reading the sheet is stamped ceartaithe, and Críochnaithe once every line is at box 4 or more. The teacher's reading reaches the script only by the pupil entering it, and README says so. Load, stated plainly: a class of 30 sends 30 cards per sheet, one sheet a half term from the second half term of Year 8 onward and two in the first; each card is 8 to 12 lines of one sentence.

proposals.approach: The next Irish class is the date, and the classroom is the conversation. Nothing is staged and the school does nothing new: a Year 8 teacher already opens most lessons by asking somebody Cad é an t-ainm atá ort?, Cá bhfuil tú i do chónaí?, Cá mhéad duine atá sa teaghlach?, and runs the same questions in pair work; those are sheet 1a and 2a. So the app stops naming a conversation the department must hold and names the thing that is on the timetable already. On the cover the pupil ticks once the days they have Irish (Luan to Aoine, a second row if the timetable runs on two weeks); departmentPages.json carries the school's term dates so the date skips Halloween, Christmas and the rest; the candidate box for Years 8 to 10 then reads Rang Gaeilge with the weekday and date of the next class after tonight. The printed sheet keeps its shape but the tick column becomes the pupil's own, headed Ráite: it lives in the jotter, the pupil ticks a line in class the moment they have said it aloud (answering the teacher, in pair work, reading their line to the partner beside them), and copies the tick into the app that night in a short strip above item 1, An rang, on the night after any class day. That tick, dated with the class, is what moves a line from box 3 to 4 and, on a later class day, from 4 to 5. Sending the sheet to the teacher is kept exactly as it stands but loses its half-term date: it is offered the night a sheet is scríofa, goes by email or Teams to the address typed on the cover, and the teacher corrects it whenever they like; the pupil types the correction as Ceartú an mhúinteora and it becomes the key. Years 11 and 12 keep Scrúdú and the exam month in the cell, and use the same class tick, since they have Irish classes too. The default calendar of pages, the four nightly items, the pen's three marks, the tier cuts, the ADHD shape, all untouched. Where it strains, honestly: a class is not a conversation, and the teacher will not ask every pupil every question, so some lines are said only in pair work or read aloud, which the tick counts because the pen cannot tell the difference; the tick is self-report, in biro, and the app says so by never marking it in the red hand; Year 10's opinion lines (cad chuige?) are asked in class less often than Year 8's facts, so Year 10 lines will climb past box 3 more slowly; phones are not out in class, so a pupil without a home printer ticks from memory that night, not on paper; a two-week timetable can drift after a holiday and needs the cover's toggle put right by the pupil; a snow day or an absent teacher makes the cell wrong for a day and the app cannot know. None of these needs the school to stage anything, and none makes a screen lie: the cell names a class that is on the timetable, and box 4 means said aloud by the pupil's own account on a dated class day, never means correct.
proposals.dateCell: All three read the same label with their own timetable's date; the tier shows elsewhere, never in the cell. Year 8 (Caoimhe, 8B, Irish on Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday, tonight Monday 28 September 2026): Rang Gaeilge: Dé Máirt 29 Meán Fómhair. Year 10 (10C, Irish on Tuesday and Thursday, same night): Rang Gaeilge: Dé Máirt 29 Meán Fómhair. The label is always Rang Gaeilge; the value is always weekday then day then month in full (Dé Luain, Dé Máirt, Dé Céadaoin, Déardaoin, Dé hAoine; Meán Fómhair, Deireadh Fómhair, Samhain, Nollaig, Eanáir, Feabhra, Márta, Aibreán, Bealtaine, Meitheamh), one format that never varies. Where the date comes from: the cover's day chips (irishDays, one row of five, or two rows with which week this is when Dhá sheachtain is on), typed once by the pupil from their timetable, and termDates in departmentPages.json (Halloween, Christmas, February, Easter, May, holy days and training days, typed once by the department in September). The app walks forward from tomorrow, skips Saturday, Sunday and any day inside a term-date range, and stops at the first weekday that is in irishDays; if no day is ticked yet it stops at the first weekday, so the cell is never blank. An optional occasion row typed from the board (cuairteoir or an Ghaeltacht with a date) replaces the cell for the seven school nights before it as Comhrá: cuairteoir, 14 Samhain, then the cell returns to Rang Gaeilge; the department promises nothing about it. proposals.whatIsPreparedFor: The Year 8 is working towards Tuesday's Irish class, the one printed on her timetable, where the teacher will ask somebody, as Year 8 teachers do at the start of nearly every lesson, Cá bhfuil tú i do chónaí? or Cá mhéad duine atá sa teaghlach?, and where in pair work she will ask and answer the same questions with the pupil beside her. That is real and it is dated: it happens on Tuesday whether or not she opens the app, and the question is on sheet 1a in her jotter with her own answer under it. A 12-year-old opens the app tomorrow night because the class is the day after, because five minutes tonight means the answer is already hers in her own words when the question lands instead of being caught out in front of the class, and because after Tuesday's class there is a box to tick on the paper and again on the screen, Ráite, that she ticks herself and nobody at school has to give her. The sheet fills line by line in biro, then fills again with ticks, and the date at the top of every screen is always a day she can count to on her fingers.
proposals.boxGate: A class tick moves a line past box 3: the pupil's own dated record that they said the line aloud in an Irish class. On the night after a class day (from irishDays and termDates), a strip above item 1, An rang, reads Rang Gaeilge inniu. Ar dhúirt tú ceann acu seo os ard? and lists at most three lines from the current sheet at box 3 or 4, the ones longest without a tick, each with a tick box in biro; the pupil copies the Ráite tick from the sheet in the jotter, or ticks from memory if nothing was printed. A tick on a box-3 line moves it to box 4 with the class date stored; a second tick on a later class day moves it from 4 to 5. Unticked lines stay where they are, nothing drops. The rewrite from memory still falls due at boxes 4 and 5 and is still marked by the pen; arís or a missed rewrite still sets the box to 0, and ticks before a reset no longer count, so a line has to climb back to 3 by writing and be said again. When every line on a sheet has a tick the sheet takes the stamp ráite (replacing ticeáilte). Why it is honest: the pen cannot judge speech, so the app never claims to; the tick is written in biro, in the pupil's own column, dated with a class that is on the timetable, and the red hand never touches it. Box 4 means said aloud by the pupil's own account, not correct; correctness is still the pen's (fadas and mutations, boxes 0 to 3) and the teacher's (the sent sheet). A pupil who ticks a line they never said gains only a longer gap before the next marked rewrite from memory, so the shortcut costs the pupil and not the record. A pupil who is never asked by the teacher can still tick a line said in pair work or read aloud to the partner beside them, which is the classroom's own conversation, the only kind the brief ever said the app owns. Nothing depends on a recording; when Abair arrives its tic and arís join on Abair é and Gan do scríbhinn only, as the brief already says, and the class tick stays.
proposals.teacherLeg: Nothing is collected and no day is promised. Seol chuig an mhúinteoir is offered the night a sheet is scríofa (every line written) and again once a teacher's correction has been typed on it, never by date; it renders the sheet as an A4 PDF (candidate box, hand line, each question in print on the left, the pupil's line beneath, a tick box Ráite for the pupil, a blank rule for the teacher, Mo cheist at the foot) into the share sheet with the teacher's address prefilled and the subject Scríbhinn 2a, Caoimhe, 8B, and stamps the sheet seolta with the date (replacing tugtha isteach). Priontáil is the second choice, for the jotter copy. Sheets arrive in the teacher's inbox or Teams drop as a trickle, one pupil at a time, and the teacher corrects in their own time in whichever way they like: reply to the email with the corrected lines, write on a printout and hand it back in class, or say it at the pupil's desk. Whatever way it comes, the pupil types it into LineView as Ceartú an mhúinteora, a draft of kind teacher that becomes the key and feeds Le ceartú, exactly as the brief has it. The app prints no return date and never shows a sheet as waiting; a sheet that is never corrected keeps the pupil's own line as its key with the pen's marks on it. The class tick and the teacher's correction are separate legs and neither waits on the other: the tick records that a line was said, the correction fixes what it said.

risks: The class tick is self-report; a pupil who ticks lines they never said reaches boxes 4 and 5 on nothing but the pen's marks on their rewrites, and the sheet's ráite stamp then overstates what was spoken.

The teacher will not ask every pupil every question; a quiet pupil's lines are said only in pair work or read aloud to a partner, which the tick counts as said, so box 4 varies in meaning from class to class.

Year 10's tier-3 opinion lines are asked in class far less often than Year 8's facts, so Year 10 lines climb past box 3 slowly and many sit at box 3, rewritten every few days, with the queue growing; the brief's design had the same saturation without the card and it is not new, but the class tick relieves it unevenly by year.
Phones are not out in class at St Paul's, so a pupil with no home printer has no paper Ráite column and ticks from memory that night, which is weaker than a tick made in the room.

The next-class date is only as true as the day chips and the term dates; a two-week timetable drifts after a holiday unless the pupil resets which week it is, and a snow day, a training day added late or an absent teacher makes the cell wrong for a day with no way for the app to know.

The sent sheet trickles into the teacher's inbox with no date; a teacher who never replies leaves the pupil's own line as the key and the pupil sees no waiting state, so uncorrected content can be rehearsed for a half term, though the pen still catches fadas and mutations.

The purpose sentence and the cover text lose the word comhrá for Years 8 to 10; the head of Irish chose the graded booklet over the conversation and may prefer the class framing, but the Year 8 and the designer chose the conversation for its date, and the class date is the only dated thing left that needs no staging.

The optional occasion row (cuairteoir, an Ghaeltacht) is a small door back to the staged conversation; if teachers type it on the board and then cancel, the cell names a day that never happens, so it must stay optional and default to nothing.
Term dates and the one-week or two-week flag are now a September dependency on the department each year; if nobody types them the date walks into Halloween week naming a class that does not exist.

proposals.approach: The pupil is the fluent speaker they prepare for. Every sheet gets its own day, Gan do scríbhinn, fixed by the app on the night the sheet is stamped scríofa: ten school nights later, counted from the department's term dates, never typed, never moved. Before scríofa the same cell shows a forecast of that day (open lines on the sheet at one a night, plus ten), printed in grey; at scríofa it is written in biro and stops moving. On the day the pupil opens Gan do scríbhinn: each question of the sheet in print, the line hidden, record, reveal, playback, then one tap, ráite (said) or arís, in rounds of three (Bliain 8) or five (from Bliain 9) with Tuilleadh anocht between rounds, unfinished rounds carrying to the next school night until every line on the sheet has been asked. The ráite tick is the pupil's own, in biro, dated; it is the only thing that moves a line past box 3, and it is never called ceartaithe. The pen keeps its three marks on writing; the teacher, from the sent sheet, and the examiner in Year 12 stay the only external checks. The staged conversation, the partner's card tick, the conversation calendar, An comhrá and the ticeáilte stamp go; Years 11 and 12 keep Scrúdú and the exam month in the cell, with the sheet's day printed on the sheet instead. Abair é on Ó chuimhne stays the nightly unmarked rehearsal; the tick lives on the day only, so ráite is one dated sitting per sheet, not a nightly self-award.

Label in every year 8 to 10: Gan do scríbhinn, followed by the sheet reference and the date, month in full in Irish; Years 11 and 12 unchanged (Scrúdú: Bealtaine 2027 for Year 12, Bealtaine 2028 for Year 11). Dates below assume term starting Tuesday 1 September 2026 and no night missed; the real table is departmentPages.json termDates.

Year 8, Caoimhe 8B: opens Thursday 3 September; nights 1 and 2 write the seven Líon an bhearna lines, night 3 (Monday 7 September) writes Q009, so 1a is scríofa 7 Meán Fómhair and its day is ten school nights on. From night 1 the cell reads, in grey (forecast), "Gan do scríbhinn: 1a, 21 Meán Fómhair"; from 7 September the same words in biro. After 21 September it reads "Gan do scríbhinn: 2a, 7 Deireadh Fómhair" (2a opened 8 September, twelve lines, scríofa 23 September, plus ten). The brief's vignette night, 6.10.26 with 2a at Líne 7 de 12, reads in grey "Gan do scríbhinn: 2a, 3 Samhain" (five lines to write, scríofa forecast 13 October, ten school nights across the half-term break).

Year 9: 1b (twelve tier-2 Mé féin questions) opened 2 September, scríofa 17 September, so "Gan do scríbhinn: 1b, 1 Deireadh Fómhair".

Year 10: 1c is Q021 alone and a sheet under three lines joins the next sheet's sitting, so the cell reads "Gan do scríbhinn: 2c, 22 Meán Fómhair" (2c, School tier 3, four lines, opened 3 September, scríofa 8 September).

Where the date comes from: the app, from two things it already holds or will hold, the sheet's scríofa stamp date and the department's term dates (a new termDates block in departmentPages.json, first and last school day of each half term, so school nights skip holidays), plus one department constant, the ten-night gap. Nothing is typed by the pupil, nothing is set by the board, and the cell is never blank because a sheet is always open and a forecast always computable. The forecast slips one night for each night missed until scríofa fixes it; after that it never moves.
proposals.whatIsPreparedFor: The Year 8 is working towards the day, a fortnight of school nights after her sheet is scríofa, when she answers the sheet's questions aloud with the questions in print in front of her and her own lines hidden, hears herself played back against each line, and ticks it ráite or sends it back with arís. It is real because it happens: a recording she makes and has to listen to, on a date the app fixed the night she finished the sheet and printed in the candidate box on every screen since; the school stages nothing, prints nothing and collects nothing on that day. It is dated because the date is a fixture, not a forecast, from scríofa on. A 12-year-old opens the app tomorrow because tomorrow's Líne nua is one more question she will be asked on that day, because the sheet fills towards it (7 de 12 scríofa, then ó chuimhne, then, on the day, the ráite column fills line by line, and Críochnaithe lands in the red hand only when every line has been written, rewritten from memory and said), and because hearing your own voice say Tá mé i mo chónaí i mBéal Feirste, and knowing whether it matched, is a small real event for a 12-year-old in a way a grey rule is not. Honestly stated: the fluent speaker she prepares for is herself, a fortnight on, and no stranger's ear is promised to her before the examiner in Year 12; the app should say that on the cover rather than pretend a conversation is coming.
proposals.boxGate: Boxes 0 to 3 stay the pen's: written, then advanced by right rewrites from memory to box 3. Box 4 needs two things on the same line: box 3 from the pen and a ráite tick from the pupil, made only on the sheet's Gan do scríbhinn day (or the nights its rounds carry to), only after the recording has been played back with the line revealed (the tic control is not shown until playback ends). A line ticked while still at box 1 or 2 carries the tick and crosses into box 4 on the rewrite that brings it to 3; a line at 3 crosses at once. Box 5 needs a second ráite on the sheet's second day, which the app sets ten school nights after every line on the sheet reaches box 4. arís sets box 0 and puts the line at the head of the queue, as now; a teacher's correction that changes the text also sets box 0 with the corrected line as key, the old ráite kept on the sheet as history. Why it is honest: the pen can check fadas, mutations and listed words in writing and nothing about speech, so the app never claims a line was said right; it records that the pupil said it, heard it, and judged it against their own line, on a date. The word is ráite (said), the tick and the sheet's ráite stamp are in the pupil's biro, not the red hand; ceartaithe is reserved for the teacher's draft and the hand never writes ráite. Críochnaithe in the hand then means: written and rewritten (the pen's word) and said (the pupil's word), and the README says so. Nothing in the gate depends on question audio; the only recording is the pupil's own, which the brief already has on Gan do scríbhinn and Abair é.
proposals.teacherLeg: Seol chuig an mhúinteoir stands as the share sheet with the teacher's address prefilled, the A4 card unchanged except that the partner's tick box becomes the ráite column, printed from the app's own record: a biro tick and the day's date on lines ticked, blank on lines sent back or not yet asked; the blank rule for the teacher and Mo cheist stay. The offer comes on the night a sheet's ráite stamp lands, once a half term by default (twice for 11 and 12 if the department sets it), and the sheet foot allows a send at any time. The flag becomes seolta (sent) with its date, not tugtha isteach, since nothing is handed in. Nothing waits on the reply: boxes, stamps, the next sheet's day and the next Seol all proceed whether or not the teacher answers. The teacher corrects in their own time by whatever means they choose (a reply to the email, a marked printout handed back in class, a word at the desk); the app cannot see any of it. The correction reaches the script the one way the brief already allows: the pupil opens the line and types it as Ceartú an mhúinteora, a draft of kind teacher that becomes the key, tapping fada, séimhiú, urú, ainm briathartha or focal for Le ceartú, or a sixth tap, Ceart mar atá, when the teacher passed the line unchanged, which marks the line ceartaithe with no draft. A typed correction sets the line to box 0 and item 1 retests it the next night with the correction printed beside it, as now. The sheet head shows seolta with its date and, once any line has a teacher draft or Ceart mar atá, ceartaithe with that date; a sheet that never comes back simply shows seolta, and the README states that the teacher's return has no day.

judgements.lens: A 12-year-old in 8B at St Paul's, three weeks into Irish, phone in hand, no exam in sight. scores.approach: 1. The sheet's own due date (Bileog 2a / faoi 23 Deireadh Fómhair), sent to the teacher, box 4 on sending, box 5 on the teacher's reading entered from the returned card
scores.bestIdea: The teacher's red pen coming back on my own sheet and me typing it in, with Ceart mar atá as one tap: the only human reading of the line in any of the three, and the only one a Year 8 actually respects. Also the fortnight rule for a pupil who installs after a date has passed, and the sheet reference in the cell so I know which sheet the date belongs to.
scores.weakestPoint: It is homework with a deadline. The thing I am preparing for is handing in, not saying anything to anyone, which is the graded booklet the Year 8 judge scored below the conversation; and the cover still says the script is for my next conversation while nothing in the app ever dates one. Box 4 on sending is thin: I press Seol whether the lines are any good or not. 23 October is four weeks away on the day I open it, which is forever to me.

scores.approach: 2. The next Irish class is the date (Rang Gaeilge: Dé Máirt 29 Meán Fómhair), the classroom is the conversation, a Ráite tick made in class and copied that night moves a line past box 3
scores.bestIdea: The date is always a day I can count to on my fingers and it is the one thing three weeks in that I actually dread: being asked Cá bhfuil tú i do chónaí? out loud on Tuesday in front of the class. Nobody at school has to do anything new. The An rang strip on the night after a class (Ar dhúirt tú ceann acu seo os ard?) is small, predictable and worth grafting whatever wins.
scores.weakestPoint: The tick is me saying I said it. I would tick everything, so would everyone in 8B, and the teacher asks one or two people a class, so most ticks are pair work or nothing. Phones are not out in class and hardly anyone prints the sheet at home, so the Ráite column in the jotter mostly does not exist. And the date is not something to work towards, it is just Tuesday; I have Irish on Tuesday whether I open the app or not, so it never lands as an event. Needs term dates typed each September and my own day chips kept right across a two-week timetable.

scores.approach: 3. The sheet's own Gan do scríbhinn day, fixed ten school nights after scríofa, the pupil records, plays back and ticks ráite; that tick alone moves a line past box 3
scores.bestIdea: The tic control is hidden until playback ends, ráite is in my biro and never in the red hand, and it is one dated sitting per sheet, not a nightly self-award. The date being fixed in biro on the night the sheet is scríofa and never moving is the right shape for the ADHD fork. All three are worth grafting.
scores.weakestPoint: The fluent speaker I am preparing for is me, three weeks into Irish, on my own phone, and nobody else ever hears it. That is not a real thing in the world; it is a thing the app made up and dated. Half of us will not record ourselves and will not listen back, and a phone without microphone permission cannot hold the day at all, so those lines stop at box 3 forever. The grey forecast that slips a night every night I miss is a small punishment before the date is even set. It drops the conversation from the cover entirely and rewrites Gan do scríbhinn into a whole new screen with rounds and a second day, which is more of the brief touched than the ruling asked for.

judgements.winner: 1. The sheet's own due date, sent to the teacher
judgements.rationale: Judged as the Year 8, proposal 2 has the date I would actually believe in (Tuesday's class, which is real and near and needs nobody to stage anything) but it hangs the whole gate on a tick I would make with my eyes shut, and the department has to keep term dates and I have to keep day chips right, so the honesty and the staging both wobble. Proposal 3 stages nothing and labels its tick honestly, but a 12-year-old does not work towards recording herself for herself, and it cuts the conversation and rewrites a screen the ruling never touched. Proposal 1 is the least exciting to me and it is homework, but the date is a real one that comes from the school's own calendar, the thing that comes back is my teacher's red pen on my own lines, which is the only reading in any proposal that is not my own word, and the app says exactly what it knows: written, sent, read. It keeps the purpose sentence, the exam end and every screen as they are. It wins on total, 16 to 15 to 14, not on excitement. For the synthesis: take proposal 1 as the base; graft proposal 2's next-class line as the near date beside the due date (or as the An rang strip on the night after a class, without any box effect); graft proposal 3's rule that no tick of any kind appears until playback ends, and that anything the pupil ticks is in biro and never in the red hand. Fix proposal 1's two soft spots: the cover must stop promising a dated conversation it cannot give, and box 4 on sending should require the sheet to be ó chuimhne on every line, not just sent. The word faoi still needs Dáithí.

judgements.lens: Head of Irish, St Paul's, the morning after telling the Principal that the department cannot hold a conversation per class each half term nor collect partner-ticked cards on a day; running this across five year groups with teachers who already mark, and who must not be handed a second marking calendar by an app.

scores.approach: Sheet due date (Bileog 2a / faoi 23 Deireadh Fómhair); sending moves box 3 to 4, the teacher's reading entered from the returned card moves 4 to 5
scores.bestIdea: Ceartú ar ais: the returned card entered per line with one tap Ceart mar atá or the teacher's line typed as the key, with seolta and ceartaithe as stamps in the hand. That is the one leg where a human who exists reads the line, and it should be grafted into the winner as an optional lift, never a required gate.
scores.weakestPoint: It is card collection on a day by another name. Thirty PDFs per class land in a teacher's inbox on 23 October because the app printed that date, and box 5 for every pupil in the school then waits on my staff replying to app-set deadlines the teacher never chose (a Friday dividing school nights in proportion to line counts is arithmetic, not a teacher's decision). Year 8 alone sends two sheets in the first half term. The proposal also contradicts itself: the boxGate counts a blank rule as Ceart mar atá while the teacherLeg says a line with no mark is left untouched.

scores.approach: Next Irish class is the date (Rang Gaeilge: Dé Máirt 29 Meán Fómhair); the pupil's own Ráite tick made on a class day moves box 3 to 4 and, on a later class day, 4 to 5; sending on scríofa with no date
scores.bestIdea: The next-class date walked from the cover's day chips and the term dates. It is the only date in the three proposals on which a fluent speaker (the class teacher) actually asks the sheet's questions aloud, it is always within days, which suits the ADHD fork, and it costs the department nothing but term dates in September.
scores.weakestPoint: The gate is a nightly self-award. An rang invites a tick on up to three lines after every class, a tick from memory is allowed when nothing was printed (phones are not out at St Paul's), nobody at school ever sees the tick, and box 5 then means only that a pupil ticked twice. The sheet's ráite stamp overstates what was spoken, and quiet pupils and Year 10's cad chuige? lines are tick-starved in ways the app cannot see. The cover text and purpose sentence, which the brief calls permanent, are rewritten, and Year 12's two cards a half term is quietly deleted.

scores.approach: Gan do scríbhinn day fixed ten school nights after scríofa; the pupil records, plays back and ticks ráite on that day only; the pupil is the fluent speaker
scores.bestIdea: The tic control is withheld until playback has ended, and ráite is one dated sitting per sheet rather than a nightly tick. Grafted onto the winner, the class tick should likewise be a sitting (one strip per class day, not per line per night) and any in-app tick should follow Abair é playback.
scores.weakestPoint: The fluent speaker is the pupil's own phone. A Year 8 who will not record herself, or whose device has no microphone permission, is stuck at box 3 with no other route, and the day is an event the app invented rather than anything outside it. It also makes tic load-bearing on Gan do scríbhinn before Abair is wired, which the brief's item 14 kept inert on purpose because there is no model to compare against; the forecast date slipping a night per missed night is exactly what the ADHD fork does not need. It rebuilds screen 5, drops the board row and removes comhrá from Years 8 to 10 entirely, so the thread is thinnest here.

judgements.winner: The next Irish class is the date, and the classroom is the conversation (proposal 2)
judgements.rationale: I said the department cannot stage a conversation or collect cards on a day. Proposal 1 hears that and hands me the same thing by email: an app-printed deadline per sheet, thirty cards per class arriving together, and a box that every pupil in five year groups cannot pass until one of my teachers has marked and returned it. The Principal called correcting in one's own time realistic; he did not say the app may print the date. Proposal 3 removes the school entirely and replaces the fluent speaker with the pupil's own phone, which is honest and dated but not real to a Year 8 in the way the brief meant, and it puts weight on tic before Abair that the brief had deliberately kept off. Proposal 2 is the only one in which the date names a day a fluent speaker will actually ask the sheet's questions, the class that is already on the timetable, and it asks the department for nothing but term dates. Its gate is weak: a nightly self-report that nobody checks. So the synthesis should keep proposal 2's date cell and An rang, graft proposal 1's Ceartú ar ais and Ceart mar atá as an optional lift (a teacher's reading, when it exists, can carry a line to box 5 and reset it on a correction, without anything waiting on it), and take proposal 3's discipline that a tick is one dated sitting, not a per-night award, ideally made after the pupil has heard themselves on Abair é. Keep the brief's purpose sentence as it stands if at all possible; the classroom is a conversation, and comhrá need not leave the cover. On Ulster forms: faoi for by, fá, and the new strings ráite, seolta, Rang Gaeilge inniu all go to Dáithí before any of it is on a screen.

judgements.lens: Product designer who rejects the generic and anything that quietly turns the booklet back into a drill app

scores.approach: 1. The sheet's own due date to the teacher (Bileog 2a / faoi 23 Deireadh Fómhair); box 4 by sending, box 5 by the teacher's reading entered
scores.bestIdea: The teacher leg as the only human reading in the loop, with a one-tap Ceart mar atá per line from the returned card, and the honest ceiling: a line whose teacher never replies stops at box 4 and the app neither fakes nor nags. That is the strongest box-5 gate of the three and should be grafted into the winner in place of a second self-tick.
scores.weakestPoint: It is homework with a deadline. The dated thing on every screen is now a submission date to a teacher, not anyone asking the pupil anything; nothing is said aloud to anyone in Years 8 to 10. The purpose sentence still promises a conversation while the header prints a hand-in date, so the thread's own words and its date cell contradict each other on every screen. The proportional-Friday due-date rule and the under-four-lines sharing rule are fussy calendar engineering that no pupil will understand, and a Year 8 who installs in November sees 1a and 2a fall due together.

scores.approach: 2. The next Irish class is the date (Rang Gaeilge: Dé Máirt 29 Meán Fómhair); the classroom is the conversation; the pupil's own dated class tick (Ráite) moves box 3 to 4 and 4 to 5
scores.bestIdea: The only proposal in which a fluent speaker still asks a Year 8 the question on the sheet, out loud, on a day the app can name without the school doing one new thing: the class is already on the timetable and the Year 8 teacher already asks Cá bhfuil tú i do chónaí? Day chips typed once by the pupil plus term dates is the cheapest honest calendar of the three. The purpose sentence 'when you are asked in Irish' covers class and exam with one phrase.
scores.weakestPoint: The gate is the pupil's word alone, and in practice not even a paper tick: phones are away at St Paul's, most Year 8s will not have printed the sheet, so 'copy the tick from the jotter' collapses into 'tick from memory the night after'. Box 5 as a second self-tick doubles the same weakness. And the An rang strip with up to three tick boxes above item 1 breaks the brief's four items, fixed order, one live: it is a checklist, which is the drill app creeping back in under a candidate box.

scores.approach: 3. Gan do scríbhinn day fixed ten school nights after scríofa; the pupil records, listens back and ticks ráite; that tick is the only way past box 3
scores.bestIdea: A date the app can own honestly: a forecast in grey that becomes biro on the night the sheet is scríofa and never moves again. That fixed-when-earned mechanic, and the rule that ráite is written in the pupil's biro and never in the red hand, are worth keeping wherever a date or a self-tick appears.
scores.weakestPoint: The pupil prepares for the app. The fluent speaker is gone from Years 8 to 10 and replaced by a test day the app sets, in rounds of three or five with tic or arís: an exam-shaped sitting per sheet for a 12-year-old, which is exactly the shape the whole-school panel rejected, and it overturns the brief's own rule that tic changes nothing until Abair is live. Any device without microphone permission, or any pupil who will not listen to themselves, stops at box 3 with no other route.

judgements.winner: 2. The next Irish class is the date; the classroom is the conversation
judgements.rationale: Only proposal 2 keeps the one thing the Year 8 and the designer voted for: somebody fluent will ask her the question on a day she can count to, and the school stages nothing because that day is already on her timetable. Proposal 1 is the graded booklet the panel scored lower, renamed: a due date to a teacher is homework, nothing is said to anyone, and the header contradicts the purpose sentence on every screen. Proposal 3 is the drill app with a candidate box on it: the app sets the test day, runs the rounds and takes the tick, and the fluent speaker the brief promised becomes the pupil herself. Proposal 2 wins on 15 to 14 to 12, but not as written. Its gate is its weakness, so the synthesis should graft in two things. From proposal 1: box 5 rests on the teacher's reading of the line, entered from the sent sheet by one tap, Ceart mar atá, or the typed correction as key, with the ceiling at box 4 if the teacher never replies; that makes the sent sheet do real work and removes the second self-tick. From proposal 3: the tick is in biro and never in the red hand, and any date the app prints is fixed once and does not drift. Two things in proposal 2 must go: the An rang strip above item 1 should be folded into the existing item 1 (Ó chuimhne on a line at box 3 the night after a class day asks Ar dhúirt tú í sa rang inniu? beneath the rewrite, one tap, no fifth thing on the page), so the four items stay four; and the optional occasion row (cuairteoir, an Ghaeltacht) should be dropped for the first build, since it is the staged conversation's back door. Purpose sentence for the synthesis: Write what you will say when you are asked in Irish, one line a night, until nothing is new. Date cell for 8 to 10: Rang Gaeilge with weekday and date in full; 11 and 12 unchanged. Decisions for Dáithí: whether the department accepts a pupil's own dated class tick as the box-4 gate given nobody at school checks it; whether each class teacher will receive sent sheets at one address and return a reading in their own time; whether the department will supply term dates and the one-week or two-week flag each September.

patch.chosen: Proposal 2, the next Irish class is the date and the classroom is the conversation, chosen by the head of Irish and the designer and top on total (45 to 44 to 38); with proposal 1's teacher leg grafted as the box-5 gate (Ceartú ar ais, Ceart mar atá, the ceiling at box 4 when the teacher never replies, sending on scríofa with no app-printed date) and proposal 3's discipline on the tick (in the pupil's biro, never in the hand, one tap per night beneath item 1 and only after Abair é has played back). The An rang strip and the occasion row are dropped, as the designer asked; the purpose sentence stands, as the head of Irish asked.
patch.purposeSentence: Write what you will say in your next conversation in Irish, one line a night, until nothing is new.

sections.heading: ## What it is for
sections.body:
Write what you will say in your next conversation in Irish, one line a night, until nothing is new.

After twenty school nights: sheet 1a in biro and rewritten from memory, sheet 2a half filled, sheet 1a sent to the teacher, the day of the next Irish class on every screen, the first lines ticked ráite the night after a class.

sections.heading: ## The thread
sections.body:
The script. One booklet belonging to one pupil from Year 8 to the exam in Year 12: twelve topic pages cut into sheets by tier, a sheet being one page's questions at one tier, in order, the same cut for every pupil, so 1a.4 is Q004 for a Year 8 and the candidate she becomes. A line is the pupil's own answer to one question, in biro, marked in the Principal's red hand for what a machine can check, sent to the teacher who corrects the rest in their own time, rewritten from memory until it is theirs.

The tier is the year a question first opens (1 in Year 8, 2 in Year 9, 3 in Year 10, exam-only in Year 11) and the grade follows the tier, not the year: Abairt amháin on tier 1 in every year; le ham nó áit on tier 2; Dhá abairt, agus cad chuige on tier 3, Freagra iomlán from Year 11. The date in the candidate box (Ainm, Rang, Líne 7 de 12, never a score) is the next time the pupil will be asked in Irish by someone fluent: for Years 8 to 10 the next Irish class on the timetable, where the teacher opens with the sheet's questions and pair work asks the rest, walked from the class days ticked once on the cover and the school's term dates; for Years 11 and 12 the exam month, the examiner last; so it is never blank and nothing is staged for it. A line is crossed through and dated only when a new draft is written over it, one more sentence in each year, so a Year 8 line sits under the Year 12 answer.

sections.heading: ## First open
sections.body:
The inside cover: Ainm; Bliain 8 to 12 with the year's rule under it; Rang (8B); the days with an Irish class, Luan to Aoine, a second row and which week this is when the timetable runs on two weeks; the year's pages, fixed for Years 8 to 10, chosen in Year 11 from the twelve; townland from the catchment list with its form after Tá mé i mo chónaí; club after Imrím le; the school's name; the teacher's address. Then sheet 1a, blank, its eight questions on the rules. The text is permanent; the fields are not.

Irish: Seo do scríbhinn féin. Ar na leathanaigh seo tá na ceisteanna a chuirfeas cainteoir Gaeilge ort sa chomhrá, agus do chuid freagraí féin orthu. Achan oíche: líne amháin nua i do chuid focal féin, agus líne a scríobh tú cheana, ó chuimhne. Ceartóidh an peann dearg na fadaí, an séimhiú agus an t-urú; is í an aip a mharcálann, i lámh an Phríomhoide. Do mhúinteoir a cheartóidh an chuid eile, ón leathanach a sheolann tú. Is é an chéad rang Gaeilge eile do chéad chomhrá eile, nuair a chuirfeas do mhúinteoir ceist ort; an scrúdaitheoir an duine deireanach a chuirfeas iad. Faoin chéad chomhrá eile ní bheidh rud ar bith le rá agat den chéad uair.

English beneath, line for line, opening: This is your own script: what you will say. The added sentence: Your next conversation is the next Irish class, when your teacher asks you a question; the examiner is the last who will ask them. Dáithí signs off the added sentence.

sections.heading: ## Home
sections.body: No home apart from the work: the app opens on Anocht, rubric Do chomhrá, scríofa agat roimh ré. Night one is one rule at a time: in Year 8, Líon an bhearna, Q001, Q002, Q006 and Q007 framed in grey from the cover and copied in biro, then Q003 to Q005 with the personal numerals in the word bank; in later years the same seven from memory, falling due one a night.

sections.heading: **1. Anocht.**
sections.body: Four items, fixed order, one live, never fewer. 1 Ó chuimhne: the most overdue line rewritten from memory, marked only on listed words missing; Abair é beneath it from box 2, unmarked until Abair; on the night after an Irish class, when the line is at box 3, one question beneath Abair é once it has played back: Ar dhúirt tú í sa rang inniu?, a tick box in the pupil's biro, dated with the class, never in the hand. 2 Focal: a word missed in item 1, else a listed word from the next question, else the next unused headword in band order, in the pupil's own sentence. 3 Foirm: the pupil's own line turned: Aimsir, another tense; Bearna, sa ______ (carr); An freagra eile, the other answer to a yes or no question; Ceist, the line's question from memory, the person shifted. 4 Líne nua, the next open question, or when none remains Líne níos fearr, the oldest line given one more sentence as a dated draft. The pen writes at most three things, glossed in grey English: fada!; a mutation note after mo, do, i, or preposition and article where the gender is known; cad chuige? on a one-sentence opinion without a reason word; bheith ag after is maith liom ag. The opener in grey on the rule; Fág go fóill twice, then Athscríobh le cuidiú; the stamp: date, one kind line, Sin é anocht.

sections.heading: **2. An scríbhinn.**
sections.body: The year's pages and open sheets, nothing grey; from Year 11 the twelve with counts. Stamps in the hand: scríofa, ó chuimhne, Críochnaithe, seolta, ceartaithe; ráite with its class date in biro beside each line. Foot action Seol chuig an mhúinteoir: the sheet as an A4 card through the share sheet to the address on the cover, offered the night the sheet is scríofa and never by a date; then Ceartú ar ais: from the card the teacher returns whenever they like, Ceart mar atá or the teacher's line, entered line by line, a line with no mark left as it is.

sections.heading: **5. Gan do scríbhinn.**
sections.body: From a sheet that is scríofa, three or five questions in print, record, reveal, playback, tic or arís, tic moving no box until Abair; the countdown from Year 11; Scrúdú béil by name only once Abair speaks.

sections.heading: **6. An clúdach istigh.**
sections.body: Details, the Irish class days, the text, Priontáil an scríbhinn ar fad, Cóip den scríbhinn, Oscail cóip, Glan an bhliain seo behind the typed name.

sections.heading: ## The years
sections.body:
Shared: all above; boxes of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 days, advanced by rewriting to box 3, to box 4 by the pupil's own ráite tick the night after a class and a right rewrite, to box 5 by the teacher's reading of the line entered from the returned sheet and a right rewrite, a line whose teacher never replies stopping at box 4; page 1, Mé féin, on every year's calendar; one Script file in iCloud across five years.

What differs:

- Year 8: tier 1; by default Mé féin and School in the first half term, Free time in the second and third, Local area and Social media after; Foirm is An freagra eile and Ceist; the pen writes fada! and mutation notes only; three questions on Gan do scríbhinn.
- Year 9: tier 2 on the same pages; Foirm adds Aimsir and Bearna; five questions.
- Year 10: tier 3 on the same pages, plus Culture and Extra-curricular; cad chuige? and bheith ag begin; the opener waits twenty seconds.
- Year 11: two pages from twelve beside page 1; Scrúdú, Bealtaine 2028 in the date cell; the countdown; the pace line above one line a night; Seol offered once a half term for a sheet with new drafts.
- Year 12: as Year 11 with Bealtaine 2027; twice a half term if the department asks.

sections.heading: ## A school night in five minutes, twice
sections.body:
Caoimhe, 8B, sheet 2a, Líne 7 de 12, Rang Gaeilge: Dé Céadaoin 7 Deireadh Fómhair. Item 1, Athscríobh 1a.3, Cá mhéad duine atá sa teaghlach?: cuigear; fada!; after Abair é plays back, Ar dhúirt tú í sa rang inniu?: she ticks, ráite 6.10.26 in biro, the tick kept until the line is rewritten right. Item 2: cúigear in her own sentence, tic. Item 3, Ceist on her 1a.4: Cá mhéad deartháir atá agam?; agat, ní agam. Item 4, Cad é mar a thagann tú ar scoil?: Tagaim ar scoil ar an bus; séimhiú de dhíth, bhus above. Stamp: 6.10.26, ar an bhus ceartaithe, maith thú, Sin é anocht.

Aoife, 12B, sheet 2c, Líne 9 de 9, Scrúdú: Bealtaine 2027. Item 1, Athscríobh 3c.2, Cad é a dhéanann tú ag deireadh na seachtaine?: peil de dhíth. Item 2: peil in her own sentence, tic. Item 3, Bearna, sa ______ (carr) from her own 2a.7: carr; charr above, séimhiú de dhíth. Item 4, An síleann tú gur rud maith í an éide scoile?: Sílim gur rud maith í. Is maith liom ag caitheamh éide scoile mar tá sé furasta ar maidin. Pen: bheith ag caitheamh. Under her 1a.4, Tá deartháir amháin agam, crossed through, 2022, the Year 9 line above it.

sections.heading: ## The exam-script register, what it must do
sections.body: Every screen must pass as a page of a candidate's script, or as the card sent to the teacher. The pen writes only what a teacher could check; the card carries the question in print, the pupil's line, the ráite tick and its date in the pupil's biro where one exists, a tick box for the teacher, Ceart mar atá, a blank rule for the teacher's correction and Mo cheist at the foot.

sections.heading: ## For a pupil with ADHD
sections.body: Progress is an object that fills: a sheet, scríofa inside a fortnight, Críochnaithe inside the half term, its ráite column filling in biro one class at a time, seolta once, ceartaithe when the card comes back, whenever that is, with nothing waiting on it. The same four items in the same order every night, one live, the class tick one tap beneath item 1 and never a fifth thing; the queue never shown. Marking is instant and glossed; one wrong form is written out again before the night closes. Le ceartú holds five things and empties. No streak, no timer until Year 11. The date at the top is always a class day the pupil can count to.

sections.heading: ## What has to be true before it can be built
sections.body: Data: the topic table; the 270 questions with gloss, tier, exam-only flag, sameAs, register, pair and opener; the department's calendar of pages, the school's term dates and whether the timetable runs on one week or two; the school's name in Irish; the catchment townlands with locatives; the verb paradigm table; a gender supplement for Year 8 words; every Irish string signed off by the Principal. Audio: none until Abair. One booklet, Years 8 to 12, in iCloud; phonics and the conversation itself are the classroom's, in the Irish class the timetable already holds; the teacher's reading reaches the script only by the pupil entering it.

sections.heading: ## Decisions only Dáithí can make
sections.body:
- Does the department accept that the date on a Year 8 to 10 screen is the next Irish class, from class days the pupil ticks once on the cover and term dates the department supplies each September, and that a pupil's own dated tick, made the night after a class, is what moves a line past box 3, given that the pen cannot judge speech and nobody at school checks the tick?
- Will each class's teacher receive sent sheets at one address, email or a Teams drop, as they come, and return a reading, a tick or a line per question, in their own time with no day the app can print, so that the pupil can enter it and a line can reach box 5?

dataListEdits: REMOVE: - The conversation calendar defaults: the partner labels (an múinteoir, Bliain 12, cuairteoir, an Ghaeltacht, an scrúdaitheoir), the rule an múinteoir on the last school night of each half term, Bliain 12 as every Year 8 class's first partner, the exam month for 11 and 12; the board's date, typed by the pupil, overrides per class; no server. Claude supplies the defaults, the department sets the real dates, Dáithí signs off. Size: 5 labels and about 6 dates a year per year group.

patch.summaryForPrincipal: For a Year 8 the date on every screen is now the next Irish class on her own timetable (Rang Gaeilge: Dé Máirt 29 Meán Fómhair), worked out from the class days she ticks once on the cover and the term dates the department supplies each September, while Years 11 and 12 keep the exam month. A line moves past box 3 when, on the night after a class, she ticks in her own biro that she said it in class today and then rewrites it right from memory, and past box 4 only when her teacher's reading of the sent sheet, a tick or a corrected line, is typed back in from the returned card, with no day promised for that and nothing else waiting on it. The school does nothing on any given day: the department types the term dates once a year, and each class teacher receives sent sheets by email or Teams as they come and corrects them whenever they like.
